analysis.one_liner: Bars meatpackers from owning, feeding, or controlling livestock before slaughter to protect independent ranchers and farmers.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to stop big meatpackers from raising their own livestock died in the Senate Agriculture Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Packers and Stockyards Act, a 1921 antitrust-style law for livestock markets, to make it unlawful for a meat packer to own, feed, or control livestock before slaughter — the practice called 'captive supply' that lets big packers buy from their own feedlots instead of the open market. Independent cattle and hog producers would have gotten a fairer chance to sell at market prices. The bill contained exemptions for small packers, farmer cooperatives, and short-term arrangements, and gave packers up to 18 months to unwind existing hog operations.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent livestock producers — cattle ranchers and hog farmers who sell on the open market — gain because packers could no longer hold large inventories of their own animals and would have to buy in open, price-reported markets. Farmers also gain bargaining room because packers could not control their farming operations through contracts.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for a packer to own, feed, or control livestock — directly, through a subsidiary, or through contracts giving the packer operational, managerial, or supervisory control — to the point that the producer no longer materially participates in managing the operation [S3].
Keeps packers from holding their own animals except in narrow cases, forcing purchases through open markets where prices are publicly reported [S3].

Carves out exemptions for farmer-owned cooperatives whose members raise and deliver the livestock themselves, small packers not required to report daily prices, and packers owning a single processing plant [S3].
Gives existing packers time to comply: swine operations have 18 months after enactment, and other livestock operations up to 180 days, rather than an abrupt cutoff [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies that rely on vertically integrated supply chains — owning feedlots or controlling contract production — bear the cost of unwinding those arrangements within 6 to 18 months. Some economists argue consumers could pay more if packers lose the efficiencies of owning their own supply, though the bill's aim was more competitive open-market pricing for producers.

drawbacks.text: The bill includes notable loopholes that blunt its reach: packers can still enter arrangements within seven days of slaughter, single-plant packers and packers exempt from daily price reporting can own or feed livestock freely, and cooperatives are exempted — all exceptions that shrink the open market it was meant to restore [S3].
Compliance deadlines (180 days to 18 months) required large packers to divest feedlots and contract arrangements on a fixed schedule, an adjustment cost the bill imposed on the industry [S3].

Critics of packer-ownership bans have long argued that forcing packers to buy everything on the spot market could raise consumer meat prices by reducing supply-chain efficiency; the bill addressed producer market fairness without directly protecting consumers from price increases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For independent ranchers and hog farmers, the benefits were substantial: an end to packer-controlled captive supply that depresses prices for animals sold on the open market. The cost fell on the four or five large packing companies that had built their businesses around owning or controlling livestock, plus a possible modest consumer price effect. The bill's own exemptions (co-ops, small packers, the 7-day window) weakened it, but the core prohibition would have meaningfully changed livestock market structure.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Grassley introduced the bill on April 15, 2005 with seven cosponsors from both parties, including Senate Agriculture Committee members Tom Harkin and a bipartisan group from farm states [S3] [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which took no further action on it [S5] [S1].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 without the bill ever leaving committee; it received no hearing, no markup, no vote, and never reached the Senate floor [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large vertically integrated meatpackers, whose packer-owned and packer-controlled livestock operations continue, and whose market position over independent producers was left untouched. Independent producers got nothing.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban packer ownership, feeding, and control of livestock

for.role: Seven senators, mostly from farm states
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Salazar, Thune, Dorgan, Enzi, Johnson, Dayton, and Harkin

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended

against.what_they_did: Long opposed packer-ownership bans, which threatened their owned feedlots and packer-controlled livestock supply

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican lead sponsor with seven cosponsors split 5 Democrats and 2 Republicans — and no recorded vote ever occurred, so the opposition was procedural: the committee simply never acted.

industries.note: The bill would have forced packers to divest owned feedlots and stop controlling producer operations, ending the captive-supply model that lets them buy from themselves instead of open markets. Its death left their market power over independent producers intact.
Producers selling on the open market would have faced fewer packer-owned animals competing with them and more transparent price discovery. They bore no cost under the bill.
Cooperatives owned by active members who raise and deliver the livestock themselves were expressly exempted from the ban, preserving their ability to market members' animals.
Packers not required to report daily prices, and packers owning one processing plant, were exempted entirely, giving them advantages over large packers under the ban.
